questions.question: The Dijkstra-Prim method finds a minimum spanning tree of a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Let $U$ be the set of vertices reached so far. Which rule does it repeat, starting from $U$ containing one vertex?
options: Add a shortest edge joining $U$ to an outside vertex, and add that vertex to $U$.
Add the shortest edge of the whole network not yet chosen, unless it closes a cycle.
Add a shortest edge from the vertex added most recently to a vertex outside $U$.
Add the outside vertex closest to the start, measured along paths, with its last edge.

questions.question: In the Dijkstra-Prim method on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, let $U$ be the set of vertices reached so far. Which edges are compared when choosing the next edge?
options: Only the edges at the vertex most recently added to the set $U$
Only the edges at the starting vertex of the method
All edges whose two endpoints both lie outside $U$
All edges joining any vertex of $U$ to a vertex outside $U$

questions.question: During the Dijkstra-Prim method, $U$ is the set of vertices already reached by the tree. Why is an edge with both endpoints in $U$ never selected, however short it is?
options: It was already compared in an earlier step and found to be too long.
Its length is already counted in the tree total through its two endpoints.
Edges inside $U$ may be used only in one direction of travel.
Its endpoints are already joined in the tree, so it would close a cycle.

questions.question: The Dijkstra-Prim method is run twice on the same connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, from two different starting vertices. Let $U$ be the set of vertices it has reached so far. What can differ between the two runs?
options: The total length, which changes with the start vertex.
The order of the edges, but not the total length.
Nothing at all: the start vertex has no effect on any step.
Only the total, never the order of the edges.

questions.question: In a step of the Dijkstra-Prim method, two different edges joining the reached set $U$ to outside vertices both have the smallest length 3. How does the method proceed?
options: The edge whose endpoint has the lower label is taken.
Either edge may be taken; the total is the same.
Both edges are taken in the same step.
The method stops, since the choice is undefined.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). The Dijkstra-Prim method starts with the reached set $U=\{B\}$. Which edge does it select first?
options: $A$–$C$, of length 2
$B$–$C$, of length 5
$B$–$A$, of length 4
$B$–$D$, of length 7

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). During the Dijkstra-Prim method the reached set is $U=\{D,F\}$, $F$ having been added last. Which edge is selected next?
options: $D$–$E$, of length 6
$E$–$F$, of length 9
$B$–$D$, of length 7
$D$–$F$, of length 4

questions.question: The Dijkstra-Prim method is applied to a connected network with 9 vertices. Let $U$ be the set of vertices it has reached so far. How many edge selections does it make before it stops?
options: 9, one for each vertex of the network
36, one for each pair of the nine vertices
8, one for each vertex added after the start
10, one per vertex plus a return edge to the start

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). Started at $A$, the Dijkstra-Prim method selects $A$–$C$, $C$–$E$, $A$–$B$, $E$–$D$ and $D$–$F$. How long is the route from $A$ to $F$ inside this tree, compared with the shortest $A$–$F$ distance in the network?
options: 14 in the tree, the same as in the network
19 in the tree, its total length, against 14
15 in the tree, against 14 in the network
4 in the tree, the length of edge $D$–$F$

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). The Dijkstra-Prim method starts with $U=\{A\}$. Which set $U$ has been reached after three edge selections?
The Dijkstra-Prim method on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths grows a set $U$ of reached vertices. Why is the set of edges it returns always a spanning tree?
options: Each edge is the shortest left in the network, and short edges never form cycles.
Each edge adds one new vertex to $U$, so no cycle forms and all vertices are joined.
A final check removes the longest edge of every cycle that has formed in $U$.
The edges may form several separate trees, which are joined once $U$ is full.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). After $A$–$C$, the reached set is $U=\{A,C\}$. Which edge does the Dijkstra-Prim method select next, and why?
options: $A$–$B$, since $B$ is 4 from $A$, while $E$ is 5 from $A$
$A$–$B$, since edges at the start vertex come first
$C$–$E$, since its length 3 is less than $A$–$B$'s 4
Both $C$–$E$ and $A$–$B$, one from each vertex of $U$

questions.question: Instead of the Dijkstra-Prim rule, a student proposes to take, at each step, the shortest unused edge of the whole network, wherever it lies. Let $U$ be the set of vertices it has reached so far. Which feature of the Dijkstra-Prim method is lost?
options: The method no longer finds the shortest edge of the network at all.
The chosen edges may no longer form one connected tree during the run.
The chosen edges would then need equal lengths before they could be compared.
The number of selected edges is no longer one less than the vertices.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). What is the total length of the tree that the Dijkstra-Prim method builds from the reached set $U=\{A\}$?

A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). After $A$–$C$ and $C$–$E$ the reached set is $U=\{A,C,E\}$. A student compares only the edges at $E$, the newest vertex, and picks $D$–$E$. Which edge does the Dijkstra-Prim method select instead?
options: $D$–$E$ (length 6)
$B$–$C$ (length 5)
$E$–$F$ (length 9)
$A$–$B$ (length 4)

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 4, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 5, $B$–$D$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $C$–$E$ 3, $D$–$E$ 6, $D$–$F$ 4, $E$–$F$ 9 (lengths after the edge names). Started from $D$ alone, the Dijkstra-Prim method grows the reached set $U$ one vertex at a time. Which edge does it add third?
options: the edge $C$–$A$, of length 2
the edge $A$–$B$, of length 4
the edge $D$–$E$, of length 6
the edge $E$–$C$, of length 3

questions.question: In the Dijkstra-Prim method on a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, the next edge $e$ is a shortest edge joining the reached set $U$ to a vertex outside. Why does adding $e$ never spoil the minimum total?
options: Some minimum tree's edge leaving $U$ can be swapped for $e$ at no extra cost.
$e$ is the shortest edge of the whole network, which every minimum tree contains.
$e$ is cheaper than every edge of the tree built so far, so it is always safe.
Adding $e$ is safe only when all edge lengths in the network are different.

questions.question: The Dijkstra-Prim method is applied, by mistake, to a network made of two separate parts with no edge between them. Let $U$ be the set of vertices it has reached so far. What happens?
options: It gets stuck: no edge leaves the reached part while vertices remain.
It joins the parts with the longest edge, as the best available.
It keeps cycling through the edges of the first part forever.
It completes normally, producing a separate tree for each of the parts.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 2, $A$–$C$ 3, $B$–$C$ 3, $C$–$D$ 1, $B$–$D$ 4. The Dijkstra-Prim method starts with the reached set $U=\{A\}$ and breaks ties arbitrarily. Which trees can it return?
options: One tree only, of total 6
Two trees, of totals 6 and 7
Three trees, all of total 6
Two trees, both of total 6

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 5, $A$–$C$ 6, $B$–$C$ 7, $C$–$D$ 8, $D$–$E$ 1, $C$–$E$ 9, $B$–$E$ 10. From the reached set $U=\{A\}$ the Dijkstra-Prim method selects $A$–$B$, $A$–$C$, $C$–$D$ and finally $D$–$E$, the shortest edge of the network. What follows about the result?
options: Its total, 20, is minimal: $D$–$E$ was out of reach earlier.
Its total, 20, would be smaller if the run started at $D$.
It is not minimal, since $D$–$E$ should have been chosen first.
Its total could be 19 by using the four shortest edges.
